exercises.title: Print a message
exercises.instructions: Write a function `say_hello()` that returns the string `'Hello, Forge!'`.
hints: Use the return keyword followed by the string in single or double quotes.
exercises.explanation: Functions return values using `return`. Quoted characters form a string in Python.

exercises.title: Work with one variable
exercises.instructions: Write a function `double_value(x)` that takes a number `x`, assigns its double to a variable `result`, and returns `result`.
hints: Use `*` for multiplication and store the answer in a variable before returning.
exercises.explanation: Assignment binds a name to the evaluated result of an expression.

exercises.title: Add two numbers
exercises.instructions: Write a function `add_numbers(a, b)` that returns the sum of `a` and `b`.
exercises.explanation: The `+` operator adds two numeric values.
exercises.reference_solution:
def add_numbers(a, b):
    return a + b

exercises.title: Compare two numbers
exercises.instructions: Write a function `is_greater(a, b)` that returns `True` if `a` is strictly greater than `b`, and `False` otherwise.
exercises.explanation: Comparison operators in Python evaluate to boolean values (`True` or `False`).
exercises.reference_solution:
def is_greater(a, b):
    return a > b

exercises.title: Check even or odd
exercises.instructions: Write a function `even_or_odd(n)` that returns `'even'` if `n` is even, and `'odd'` if `n` is odd.
hints: Use modulo operator `% 2 == 0` to check for even numbers.
exercises.explanation: An integer is even if divided by 2 leaves no remainder (n % 2 == 0).

exercises.title: Count positive numbers
exercises.instructions: Write a function `count_positives(nums)` that counts how many numbers in a list `nums` are strictly greater than 0.
hints: Initialize a counter variable to 0, loop through `nums`, and increment when `num > 0`.
exercises.explanation: Accumulating counts using a loop is the foundation of iterative algorithms.

exercises.title: Find a maximum manually
exercises.instructions: Write a function `find_max(nums)` that takes a non-empty list of integers and returns the largest value by iterating through it.
hints: Set `max_val = nums[0]` before looping so negative values are handled correctly.
exercises.explanation: Initializing with the first element guarantees correct comparison across all number ranges.

exercises.title: SELECT a constant
exercises.instructions: Write a query that selects the integer `42` with column alias `answer`.
exercises.explanation: SQL can evaluate and project scalar expressions without touching a table.

exercises.title: Read one column
exercises.instructions: Select only the `title` column from the `books` table.
exercises.setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE books (id INT PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT, author TEXT);
INSERT INTO books VALUES (1, 'Clean Code', 'Robert Martin'), (2, 'The Pragmatic Programmer', 'David Thomas');

examples.output:
| title |
| Clean Code |
| The Pragmatic Programmer |

exercises.explanation: Projection retrieves only the requested columns, saving bandwidth and memory.

exercises.title: Filter with WHERE
exercises.setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, is_active BOOLEAN);
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'Alice', true), (2, 'Bob', false), (3, 'Charlie', true);

examples.input: SELECT name FROM users WHERE is_active = true;

hints: Add `WHERE is_active = true` at the end of the query.
exercises.explanation: The WHERE clause acts as a predicate filtering table rows before projection.
exercises.reference_solution: SELECT name FROM users WHERE is_active = true;

exercises.title: Check for NULL values
exercises.instructions: Select `id` and `name` from `customers` whose `phone` is NULL.
exercises.setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE customers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, phone TEXT);
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1, 'Dev', NULL), (2, 'Priya', '9876543210'), (3, 'Sam', NULL);

examples.input: SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE phone IS NULL;

hints: In SQL, test for missing data using `IS NULL`, never `= NULL`.
exercises.explanation: NULL represents missing information; standard equality comparisons with NULL yield UNKNOWN.
exercises.reference_solution: SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE phone IS NULL;

exercises.title: Trace and sum a list
exercises.instructions: Write a function `sum_list(elements)` that computes the sum of numbers in `elements` without using the built-in `sum()` function.
hints: Use a running total variable initialized to 0 and loop over each item.
exercises.explanation: Sequential accumulation is the simplest linear scanning pattern.

exercises.title: Linear search for index
exercises.instructions: Write a function `find_index(elements, target)` that returns the 0-based index of the first occurrence of `target` in `elements`, or `-1` if it is not present.
hints: Use `for i, x in enumerate(elements):` and return `i` immediately when `x == target`.
exercises.explanation: Linear search inspects elements from left to right with O(n) time complexity.

exercises.title: Frequency counting with a dictionary
exercises.instructions: Write a function `build_counts(items)` that returns a dictionary mapping each element to how many times it appears in `items`.
hints: Check `if item in counts:` or use `counts.get(item, 0) + 1`.
exercises.explanation: Frequency counting using hash maps enables O(1) lookups for anagram and duplicate checks.
